chunks: From him, from Ibn Ribāṭ, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said:

At times I would enter upon Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام after I had prayed ẓuhr and ʿaṣr, and he would say: “Have you prayed ẓuhr?” I would say: “Yes, and ʿaṣr.” Then he would say: “I have not prayed ẓuhr.” So he would rise calmly, not hurrying, and perform ghusl or wudu (ablution), then pray ẓuhr and then pray ʿaṣr. And at times I would enter upon him while I had not prayed ẓuhr, and he would say: “You have prayed ẓuhr?” I would say: “No.” Then he would say: “I have already prayed ẓuhr and ʿaṣr.”

It was said to him: “There is nothing in these reports that conflicts with what we have previously presented, because his statement عليه السلام, ‘All of that is broad in allowance,’ is to be understood as meaning that all of it is permissible, having been allowed by the Shariʿah, even if some of its forms have merit over others. And there is nothing in the report to indicate that all of that broad allowance is equal in merit. It is also possible that he allowed that for them due to a certain kind of expediency and taqiyyah; this is indicated by that.”

key_terms.وَاسِعٌ: broad in allowance; religiously permitted within a range
key_terms.ٱلتَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation/precautionary concealment for protection or expediency
key_terms.ٱلشَّرِيعَةُ: the sacred law that grants the permissibility

ai.seo_question: Does this hadith show that the time for ẓuhr and ʿaṣr salat (prayer) is flexible in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This report discusses the timing of ẓuhr and ʿaṣr salat (prayer), showing that both early and delayed performance could fall within a permitted range. The concluding scholarly note explains that permissibility does not necessarily mean equal merit, and that some allowances may also relate to expediency or taqiyyah.
